q: Lithium is added to a trough of water. Which observation is correct?
options: It floats and fizzes steadily as a gas is produced.
It sinks and dissolves without bubbles.
It melts into a ball and burns with a lilac flame.
It stays unchanged on the surface.
explain: Lithium floats on water and fizzes steadily as hydrogen gas is made. It does not melt or ignite.

q: Which statement about transition elements as catalysts is correct?
options: They are never used as catalysts.
They are often used as catalysts as elements and in compounds.
Only their compounds, not the elements, can act as catalysts.
They are used up when they act as catalysts.
explain: Both transition elements and their compounds are often catalysts, for example iron and manganese(IV) oxide.

q: An atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. Which row gives its position in the Periodic Table?
explain: Six outer electrons place it in Group VI, and three occupied shells place it in Period 3.

q: Which halide ion is displaced from solution by both chlorine and bromine?
explain: Iodide is the least reactive halogen of these, so both chlorine and bromine, being more reactive, displace it as iodine.

q: Why can iron form two different chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃?
options: It has different numbers of protons in each compound.
It is a Group II element.
It can form ions with different charges.
It forms molecules rather than ions.
explain: Transition elements like iron can lose different numbers of electrons, forming Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
options: Their atoms have the same number of electron shells.
Their atoms have the same number of protons.
Their atoms have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
Their atoms have the same relative atomic mass.
explain: Chemical reactions involve outer electrons, so the same number of outer electrons gives similar reactions.

q: Which formula represents helium gas?
explain: Helium is monatomic, so its formula is simply He.

q: The noble gases are in Group VIII. Which statement about the elements in this group is correct?
options: They are all liquids at r.t.p.
They are all solids at r.t.p.
They are all gases at r.t.p.
explain: The elements of Group VIII, from helium to radon, are gases at room temperature.

q: Which statement about halogens is correct?
explain: Halogens consist of non-metal atoms joined in pairs by covalent bonds.

q: Which halogen is the most reactive of chlorine, bromine and iodine?
explain: Reactivity decreases down the group, so chlorine, at the top, is the most reactive of the three.

q: Sodium has a relative atomic mass of 23. What volume of hydrogen at r.t.p. is made when 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water? (1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)
explain: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂: 2.3 g = 0.10 mol Na gives 0.050 mol H₂, which is 0.050 × 24 = 1.2 dm³.

q: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a neon atom?
explain: Neon is 2,8, so its outer shell holds 8 electrons.

q: How does the reactivity of the halogens change down Group VII?
explain: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine.

q: What is the appearance of iodine at r.t.p.?
explain: Iodine is a grey-black solid at r.t.p.

q: Elements in Group V (such as nitrogen) form ions with a charge of
explain: Group V atoms have 5 outer electrons and gain 3 electrons to complete the shell, forming 3− ions.

q: A halogen X₂ does not react with aqueous sodium chloride or aqueous sodium bromide, but it does react with aqueous sodium iodide. What is X₂?
explain: Bromine does not displace chloride or bromide ions, but it displaces iodide. Only bromine fits all three results.

q: 4.6 g of sodium (Aᵣ = 23) reacts completely with water. What mass of sodium hydroxide (Mᵣ = 40) is formed?
explain: 4.6 g is 0.20 mol Na; 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ gives 0.20 mol NaOH; 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g.

q: Which statement compares atoms of lithium, sodium and potassium?
options: They have a different number of outer electrons but the same number of shells.
They have the same number of shells and the same number of protons.
They have the same number of protons but a different number of outer electrons.
They have the same number of outer electrons but a different number of shells.
explain: Group I atoms each have one outer electron; each lower element has one more occupied shell.

q: Chlorine gas is bubbled through aqueous potassium bromide. What is seen?
explain: Chlorine displaces bromine, because it is more reactive. Aqueous bromine is orange-brown.

q: Iron reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride. Which equation is correct?
explain: Two Fe and six Cl are required on each side for balance, so 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃.

q: How does the melting point change down Group I from lithium to potassium?
explain: The melting points are lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C and potassium 63 °C, so they decrease down the group.

q: Which block of elements lies between Group II and Group III in the Periodic Table?
explain: The transition elements form a central block between Groups II and III in the long periods.

q: An element has proton number 12. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
explain: Proton number 12 gives the configuration 2,8,2: two outer electrons (Group II) in three shells (Period 3).

q: Which element forms an ion with a charge of 1−?
explain: Fluorine is in Group VII and gains one electron to form F⁻. Oxygen forms 2− ions, sodium forms 1+ ions and neon forms no ions.

q: Which compound is likely to be coloured?
explain: Compounds of transition elements are coloured; compounds of Group I and II elements are generally white.

q: Element P does not displace chlorine from aqueous sodium chloride but does displace iodine from aqueous sodium iodide. Which could P be?
explain: P is less reactive than chlorine but more reactive than iodine, so it lies between them in Group VII: bromine.

q: A newly discovered element has atoms with 7 outer electrons and 5 occupied electron shells. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
explain: Outer electrons give the group number (VII) and the number of occupied shells gives the period (5).

q: Which statement describes how sodium differs from a typical transition element such as iron?
options: Sodium is harder and has a higher melting point.
Sodium is softer and has a lower melting point.
Sodium is denser and has a higher melting point.
Sodium is softer and has a higher melting point.
explain: Group I metals are soft with low melting points; iron is hard with a high melting point.

q: Which statement about the density of Group I metals is correct?
options: All Group I metals are denser than iron.
Lithium is much less dense than water.
Lithium sinks in water because it is dense.
Densities decrease strongly from lithium to caesium.
explain: Lithium has a very low density (0.53 g/cm³) and floats on water; the general trend is an increase down the group.

q: Which prediction about astatine, At, below iodine in Group VII, is most likely to be correct?
options: It is more reactive than chlorine.
It would displace iodine from potassium iodide.
It is a pale-coloured gas at r.t.p.
It is less reactive than iodine.
explain: Reactivity decreases down Group VII, and the elements become darker solids, so At is less reactive than I.
